newsitem.title: CHINA: Exiles say two Uighurs face execution in China.
newsitem.headline: Exiles say two Uighurs face execution in China.

text.p: Uighur exiles said on Wednesday that China planned to execute two religious students from the Moslem ethnic group on Thursday. The pair were arrested last month in connection with riots in China's Xinjiang province.

"Two young men, accused of leading the February events, will be executed tomorrow," Mukhiddin Mukhlisi, spokesman for the United National Revolutionary Front of East Turkestan, told Reuters in Almaty, the capital of neighbouring Kazakhstan.

Information from the remote, closed region of mountain and desert is difficult to verify. Uighur exiles say telephone lines to Xinjiang have been cut, and news often arrives days late via traders crossing the China-Kazakh border.

Mukhlisi, who said he received the information on the executions from his organisation's "secret sources", named the two Uighurs as Abu Khair and Abdu Medchit, both around 25 years old and religious students in Yining.
The two would probably face a firing squad in Urumqi, regional capital of Xinjiang, Mukhlisi said.
He said the two were arrested on February 7 in Yining, near the border with Kazakhstan and scene last month of some of the most violent disturbances in the province since the 1949 communist takeover.
The Front is one of several Uighur organisations fighting for an independent "East Turkestan" in Xinjiang, home to a majority of Turkic-speaking Moslems like the ethnic Uighurs.
"These executions could provoke more bloodshed in the province," Mukhlisi warned.

Exile groups said last month the Yining riots were sparked by the execution of about 30 Uighurs by the Chinese authorities. Chinese sources said about 10 people were killed and 100 wounded in the resulting disturbances.
Bomb attacks followed in Urumqi and the Chinese capital Beijing in late February and earlier this month.

Last year, the Xinjiang authorities cracked down on Uighur secessionists after a series of violent clashes, bombings and assassination attempts on officials and Moslem leaders regarded as pro-Beijing.
The Chinese authorities also toughened their border regime, saying Uighur groups were smuggling arms across the frontier from the former Soviet republics of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.
Uighur groups say the neighbouring ex-Soviet states -- which share a Turkic language, Islam and a nomadic heritage -- have fuelled Uighur dreams of independence.

But, anxious about their own territorial integrity, the Central Asian states are unlikely to push the Uighur issue when they meet Chinese and Russian officials in Moscow next month to sign a troop reduction pact along their common frontiers.
